root.note: The stone came first, then the colour. Sources differ on the road to Spanish: through Old French azur (Wiktionary), or straight from a colloquial Arabic lāzūrd (Corominas, via dechile.net).

history: Spanish azul is a colour named after a stone. Persian lāžvard was lapis lazuli, the deep-blue gem, and Arabic made it lāzaward. Somewhere on the road west the first l was lost. Sources disagree about the route. Wiktionary sends it through Medieval Latin lazulum and Old French azur, Corominas through colloquial Arabic. Azure in English is a relative, and lapis lazuli still names the stone. Don't be fooled by azulejo, though. The famous Spanish tile is not named for blue. It comes from Arabic az-zulayj, ‘polished stone’, and only looks related.
historyEinfach: Azul means ‘blue’. The word comes from Persian. In Persian, it was the name of a deep-blue stone: lapis lazuli. Arabic took the name, and later Europe took it too. Experts don't agree on the road to Spanish. Careful: azulejo, a Spanish tile, looks related to azul. It is not. It comes from an Arabic word for a smooth stone.

cognates.note: A tile, from Arabic az-zulayj ‘polished stone’

elsewhere.text: It looks like ‘a little blue thing’, and many people think so. The Arabic origin says otherwise.
English azure is related to the Spanish word, and lapis lazuli is its stone.
Persian lâjvard still names the stone, which started all this.
